hook.text: Swahili is a Bantu language seasoned with Arabic, Persian, and Portuguese—a trade-route creation.

buildup.text: Indian Ocean merchants needed a shared tongue. Swahili emerged along the East African coast by 200 AD.

discovery.text: After independence, Tanzania chose Swahili as its national language to unite 120 ethnic groups under one voice.

twist.text: Today over 100 million people speak Swahili. It's the African Union's official working language.

climax.text: Swahili proves a lingua franca doesn't need a colonial origin. Trade and choice can build one organically.

punchline.text: Commerce built more shared languages than conquest.

quiz.question: Which country chose Swahili to unite 120 ethnic groups?

details.summary: Swahili grew from an East African coastal trade language to the African Union's first African lingua franca. It is spoken by over 100 million people across multiple nations.
details.whyItMatters: Swahili's rise demonstrates that African languages can serve as national and international languages. It challenges the assumption that only European languages can unify diverse populations.
takeaways: Swahili is spoken by over 100 million people across East Africa
Tanzania successfully made Swahili its national language post-independence
Swahili became the African Union's official language in 2004

faq.question: How did Swahili become so widely spoken?
faq.answer: Swahili originated as a trade language on the East African coast, blending Bantu structure with Arabic vocabulary. Arab and Portuguese traders spread it along trade routes. German and then British colonizers adopted it as an administrative language.

faq.question: Why is Swahili significant for pan-Africanism?
faq.answer: Most African nations use colonial European languages as their lingua franca. Swahili is the rare exception — an indigenous African language that serves this function.
